posts.name: Statistics Canada
posts.content: Statistics Canada: The Consumer Price Index rose 3.1% year over year in September 2026, up from 3.0% in August. Gasoline prices were up 27.8% on the year. Excluding gasoline, CPI rose 2.2%, down from 2.4% in August.

posts.name: the Bank
posts.content: Bank of Canada reminder: The next interest rate announcement and Monetary Policy Report will be released Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at 9:45 a.m. ET. Governor Tiff Macklem and Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers will hold a press conference at about 10:30 a.m. ET.

posts.name: The Hub
posts.content: Brent crude has settled at US$113.17, far above the roughly US$75 assumed in the Bank of Canada's July outlook. The October MPR will have to reckon with an oil shock the Bank's previous forecasts did not anticipate. Does that force a hike, or does the Bank look through an energy-driven supply shock?

posts.name: Reuters
posts.content: Reuters poll: Ahead of the October 28 Bank of Canada decision, 15 of 34 economists surveyed do not forecast a rate hike. Respondents see Q3 GDP growth at about 1.9%, slowing to 1.3% in Q4, as US tariffs weigh on activity. Oil traded at US$117 on Friday.

posts.name: Sherry Cooper
posts.content: The September CPI report did nothing to advance the case for interest rate hikes. Strip out gasoline and inflation is 2.2% and falling, and core measures eased. With tariffs biting, the Bank has every reason to stay at 2.25% on October 28.

posts.name: Economists surveyed
posts.content: A hike next week is not a slam dunk, but there is probably enough supporting evidence for one. Headline inflation is above 3%, oil is well north of the Bank's assumptions, and the Fed and ECB have both tightened. The Bank told us in September that upside risks had increased.

posts.name: CIBC
posts.content: Desjardins is switching to a rate-hike call for the Bank of Canada. Persistent energy-driven inflation, rising inflation expectations and global tightening tilt the balance toward a 25 bp increase from 2.25%.

posts.name: Andrew Grantham
posts.content: Policymakers have time before raising rates. Our base case remains a first hike in January 2027, though it could come earlier. Weakening growth from tariffs argues for patience on October 28.

posts.name: Tiff Macklem
posts.content: If the new US tariffs remain in place, fourth-quarter growth could be roughly halved to below 1%. We remain focused on preventing higher energy prices from feeding into broader inflation, and we are prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed.

posts.content: With oil above $110 and gas prices up nearly 28%, is the Bank of Canada really going to hike into a tariff slowdown? My mortgage renewal is coming up. Hold or hike on Wednesday?

posts.name: Standard Chartered
posts.content: Bank of Canada preview: our base case is a hold at the 28 October decision, leaving the policy rate at 2.25%. The announcement is at 9:45 a.m. ET alongside the new Monetary Policy Report, with Governor Macklem and Senior Deputy Governor Rogers at about 10:30 a.m. ET. Tariff-driven growth weakness argues for patience. Cost pass-through and expectations argue against easing. We see the balance of risks as two-sided, so guidance tone matters as much as the decision. We will focus on MPR oil assumptions versus the July outlook and on whether underlying inflation is broadening. We are not dismissing a hike, and the risks around the call are real. Content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice.

The 50% tariffs on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods reflect the lack of an acceptable agreement, not hostility toward the Canadian people. Our partners must do their part. Canada should return to the table with serious proposals that protect American workers and create fair and reciprocal trade. America First.

posts.name: Peter Shannon
posts.content: Decision week preview: we expect the Bank of Canada to hold at 2.25% on 28 October. Brent near US$113 against the roughly US$75 assumed in July is the key input for the October MPR. Three things we'll be watching: the Bank's revised oil assumption, whether firms' pass-through plans broaden into core prices, and the forward guidance at the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference. Risks are tilted toward a later hike if second-round effects build. For businesses, the takeaway is to plan on a hold but stress-test costs and financing at a higher rate path. General information only, not investment advice. #BankofCanada #CdnEcon

posts.name: Economists surveyed
posts.content: Reuters poll of 34 economists, 21–23 October 2026, ahead of the Bank of Canada decision on Wednesday 28 October. The policy rate is 2.25%. 15 of 34 did not forecast a rate hike. The remaining 19 expected tightening, a narrow implied majority for a hike. Upside risks cited: energy pass-through, and Bank surveys showing rising consumer long-term inflation expectations and about half of firms planning to pass on cost increases. Downside risks cited: US tariffs on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, September employment down 68,000 and unemployment at 6.5%. Poll GDP estimates are about 1.9% in Q3 and 1.3% in Q4 2026. Announcement 9:45 a.m. ET with the MPR; press conference about 10:30 a.m. ET. General information, not investment advice.

posts.name: Carolyn Rogers
posts.content: Reminder: the Bank's interest rate announcement and the October 2026 Monetary Policy Report are released Wednesday, 28 October at 9:45 a.m. ET, with the press conference at about 10:30 a.m. ET. The statement and report will be published at bankofcanada.ca, and key messages will also be available in French. We will not comment on the decision before it is announced, so please read the primary documents before relying on forecasts or headlines.

posts.name: Economists polled by Reuters
posts.content:
Reuters poll, 34 economists polled October 21–23, 2026: 19 expect the Bank of Canada to hike 25 bp to 2.50% on October 28. The other 15 do not forecast a move from the current 2.25% policy rate. A narrow majority expects tightening, so the panel is split and uncertainty is elevated.

Context from public sources: September CPI rose 3.1% y/y, or 2.2% excluding gasoline. Brent has traded well above US$110, compared with about US$75 in the Bank's July outlook. The poll's median estimates are about 1.9% GDP growth in Q3 and 1.3% in Q4.

Either outcome would surprise a large share of forecasters. Consensus summarises information. It does not guarantee an outcome. Announcement is 9:45 a.m. ET, with the press conference at about 10:30 a.m. ET.

posts.name: Derek Holt
posts.content: Bank of Canada decision on 28 October: my call is a 25 bp hike from 2.25%. It is not a slam dunk. The case rests on three things. First, Brent at about US$113 against the roughly US$75 July assumption means the October MPR oil path has to reset. Second, about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter cannot say when inflation returns to 2%. That is unanchoring risk, not noise. Third, headline CPI is above 3%. The offset is real: ex-gasoline CPI eased to 2.2%, and growth is slowing toward roughly 1.3% in Q4 on US tariffs. I think the balance of risks still favours acting now rather than waiting for second-round effects to show up in the data. What would change my mind: a clearly lower oil assumption in the MPR, or a softer tone on expectations at the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference. General information only, not investment advice.

posts.name: Sherry Cooper
posts.content:
Bank of Canada preview, decision Wed 28 Oct (9:45 a.m. ET, with the October MPR). My base case is a hold at 2.25%.

The dilemma is genuine. Oil is far above the ~US$75 assumed in July (Brent settled at US$113.17 on 22 Oct), and about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases. Those are real upside inflation risks. But tariffs are slowing growth (Reuters poll: Q3 ~1.9%, Q4 ~1.3%), and CPI excluding gasoline eased to 2.2% in September, with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%.

Hiking into a tariff-hit, slowing economy would be a policy error unless expectations clearly de-anchor. I'm watching the forward guidance at the 10:30 a.m. presser closely, and I'll update my view if the data change.

For renewals: variable rates follow the policy rate directly. Fixed rates follow the 5-year GoC yield, which has already moved up. Run your payment under hold, +25 bp and +50 bp scenarios before you decide. This is my read, not a rate promise. Stay tuned.

posts.name: The Hub
posts.content: The number that matters: September CPI rose 3.1% year over year, but excluding gasoline it rose 2.2%, down from 2.4% in August. Gasoline was up 27.8% on the year, so energy is doing most of the work in the headline. The question for the Bank of Canada ahead of 28 October is whether underlying pressure is broadening, not whether gasoline is rising. Source: Statistics Canada.

posts.name: User
posts.content:
Read the resolution criteria before you argue about the 28 October decision. Thread for the October 2026 Bank of Canada question:

1. Decision: Wed 28 Oct 2026, announcement 9:45 a.m. ET with the October MPR. Press conference about 10:30 a.m. ET.
2. Baseline: target rate 2.25%, in place since 29 Oct 2025. The Bank sets a single target rate, not a range, so the upper-bound clause in the generic template does not apply here.
3. "No change" only if the rate is still exactly 2.25% after the 28 October announcement.
4. Any increase or decrease counts as a change. Moves under 25 bp are rounded up to 25 bp, so a 10 bp move is a 25 bp change, not "no change."
5. Larger moves round to the nearest 25 bp, with ties away from zero.
6. Emergency moves outside the scheduled announcement do not count.
7. If the announcement is postponed, the decision still counts if it comes before the next scheduled decision on 9 Dec 2026. If it is cancelled, or no decision is made before 9 Dec, the question resolves "no change."
8. The summary of deliberations should follow about two weeks after 28 October. The 2 September decision summary came out on 16 September.

Edge cases are where questions go to die. Exactly means exactly.

The hike camp's strongest evidence is the expectations side: about half of firms plan to pass on costs, and nearly a quarter cannot say when inflation returns to 2%. The hold camp's strongest evidence is the core side: CPI ex-gasoline at 2.2%, CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%, with Q4 growth near 1.3%. Dispersion like this is itself information. The 10:30 a.m. ET press conference and the October MPR oil assumptions should show which weighting the Bank is using. General information only.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: I agree the dilemma is genuine, but I'd frame the policy-error risk the other way round. Waiting for expectations to clearly de-anchor means the Bank acts after second-round effects are already in pricing. Firms are signalling it: about half plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter cannot say when inflation returns to 2%. Ex-gasoline CPI at 2.2% is useful, but it is a lagging read on a shock that has not finished feeding through. Growth near 1.3% in Q4 is a real drag, which is why I'd take 25 bp rather than 50. The 10:30 a.m. ET presser will tell us which risk the Bank is more worried about.

comments.name: Scotiabank
comments.content: Respect to Desjardins for setting out the hike case clearly. Our economists also lean toward further tightening on 28 October, though it is not a slam dunk. The strongest evidence is on expectations: about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter cannot say when inflation returns to 2%. Brent near US$113 against the roughly US$75 in the Bank's July outlook also makes the MPR assumptions a live question. The hold case rests on softer core readings and tariff drag on Q4 growth, which is why this is close. Views are our economists' own and subject to revision. Read the full note for the data.

comments.name: CIBC
comments.content: Our view is that the trade-off is now mainly about breadth. If tariffs keep Q4 growth below 1%, the case for patience gets stronger. The key test is whether energy-driven price increases spread into core inflation and expectations. We will be watching the October MPR and the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference for how the Bank weighs the two. General information only, not investment advice.

comments.name: Leslie Preston
comments.content: Agree the split is real, and it reflects genuine two-sided risk. Our base case is a hold at 2.25% on October 28. Core evidence has cooled (CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9% in September), and Q4 growth near 1.3% argues against tightening. The hawkish case is credible, though: oil is well above the roughly US$75 July assumption, and about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases. What would change our view is broadening in core prices and inflation expectations moving clearly off 2%. We'll be reading the MPR oil assumptions closely at 9:45 a.m. ET. This is a forecast, not a guarantee.

comments.name: The Hub

We will watch the MPR oil assumption against the July outlook and the tone at the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference. This is a forecast, not a recommendation.

comments.name: Dominion Lending

comments.name: User
comments.content:
Two things I'd check before reading the MPR as a verdict on oil:

1. Whether the Bank resets its oil assumption. The July outlook used roughly US$75 Brent. Settlement at US$113.17 is a gap of about US$38 a barrel, so the October MPR path is the first document to read.
2. Whether second-round effects show up. The signal I'd weight most is firms' pricing plans and expectations, not the headline oil price.

A hold on 28 October leaves the rate exactly at 2.25%, which is "no change" under the resolution criteria. Any move, even 10 bp, counts as a change (rounded up to 25 bp). Read the criteria before arguing about edge cases.
